title: Make a role's invocation match the grant it holds, and protect the args-derivation property in CI

history.detail:
CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL — round 1. Audited 17461bb on main; working tree clean apart from .vscode/settings.json. Sprint file read fresh at audit time.

Reqs 1, 2, 3 and 5 are met, and Req 2 is met in the strong sense the criterion asks for. Req 4 is not, and I can show it: the defect that requirement exists to guard against can be present with your entire suite green.

================================================================
BLOCKER — REQ 4. THE CI TEST DOES NOT PROTECT THE PROPERTY IT NAMES.
scripts/launcher_test.js:2501 (the Sprint 31 Req 4 test)
================================================================

Req 4: "the emitted record is derived from the values actually passed to the child rather than reassembled from a second source — is protected by a test that runs in CI." The criterion closes: "A test that recomputes what it is checking would pass while the defect it guards against is present."

I introduced exactly that defect and ran the suite. One edit, in emitPermissionRecord, replacing the args-derived allowedTools with one rebuilt from HEADLESS_PERMISSION_PROFILES — the literal "second source" the requirement names:

    allowedTools: HEADLESS_PERMISSION_PROFILES[role.id].allowedTools.join(' ')

    node scripts/launcher_test.js  ->  ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED

Not just your Req 4 test. The whole suite. The record was reassembled from a second source and nothing in CI noticed.

WHY, and this is the part that matters: in this repo the profile-joined string and the args string are byte-identical for all six roles. No fullyCompletely.testCommand is declared and no ownedRepository grant is in force, so needsTestCommand and the owned-repository branch both append nothing. Two sources that produce the same bytes cannot be told apart by any comparison between them — including a comparison against the child's real argv, because the child received that same identical string. The test compares a value to itself by a longer route.

TO BE FAIR TO THE LETTER OF THE CRITERION: the test does assert against values passed to the child, it does not compare the record to a recomputation of the record, and it does run under `node scripts/launcher_test.js`, which .github/workflows/scan.yml:45 genuinely executes. Every clause reads as satisfied. The requirement's substance — protection — is what is absent, and protection is what Req 4 asks for. This is the same shape as the note I left on sprint 30 and it is why I left it: the fix chosen made the test cross a real subprocess boundary, which is a genuine strengthening in a different dimension (it caught the missing-instruction mutation below, in-process tests and all), but it does not address the dimension the requirement is about.

THE FIX, AND I CLEARED THE OBSTACLE IN FRONT OF IT RATHER THAN HANDING YOU ONE THAT DOESN'T WORK. The two sources have to actually differ before any test can distinguish them. The way to make them differ is a declared test command, which appends a third entry for a needsTestCommand role. My first attempt at that failed, and the reason is worth knowing:

    headlessLaunchArgs(role, prompt, { root })  ->  headlessPermissionArgs(role)   // root NOT passed

`root` is threaded to readDeclaredMcpConfig(root) four lines below and never to headlessPermissionArgs, so withScratchSettings can declare a test command all day and the permission args still read the real ROOT. That is pre-existing, from sprint 12 (4372ad0), not yours — but it is what blocks the test Req 4 needs.

I tried the one-token fix and checked it for fallout before recommending it:

    ...headlessPermissionArgs(role, root)]
    node scripts/launcher_test.js  ->  ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED   (no fallout)

and with it threaded, a scratch root declaring "node scripts/launcher_test.js" produces:

    args    : Bash(node scripts/run-lifecycle.js *) Bash(python3 scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py *) Bash(node scripts/launcher_test.js *)
    profile : Bash(node scripts/run-lifecycle.js *) Bash(python3 scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py *)

They differ. Then I re-applied the second-source drift on top and the comparison finally fails:

    record === args ?  false      <- the drift is now detectable

So: thread `root` (which also fixes a real half-honored option, since production always passes ROOT and behaviour is unchanged there), then add a test that launches a needsTestCommand role against a scratch root with a declared test command and asserts record.allowedTools equals the args value. Three small pieces, all three verified working here.

Note the subprocess test can't be the one to carry this — ROOT is fixed from __dirname in a real child, so a scratch root can't reach it without copying the tree. Keep your subprocess test exactly as it is, it protects something real; add the divergence check in-process alongside it.

================================================================
WHAT IS MET, AND REQ 2 IS THE BEST WORK IN THIS SPRINT
================================================================

REQ 2 — "a reviewer should be able to point at the single source, not at two places that currently agree." I did the experiment the criterion describes rather than reading for it. One edit, inside HEADLESS_PERMISSION_PROFILES only, adding 'Bash(qa1-invented-command *)' to master-controller:

    prompt instruction now names it            : true
    record.instructedCommandForms              : [..., "qa1-invented-command"]
    grep for a second literal of that form     : exactly one hit, line 840, the profile itself

One edit, both consumers changed, no second literal anywhere in scripts/. That is the single source, demonstrated. extractGrantedCommandForms reads the already-assembled --allowedTools string rather than the profile that built it, which is why a dynamically-added grant is swept in identically — the right level to parse at.

REQ 1 — verified across the subprocess boundary, all six roles, with my own regex written in the probe rather than importing yours, against the argv a real child process actually received:

  role                forms   instruction first   every form named   task still present
  master-controller     2           yes                 yes                yes
  dev-team-1            2           yes                 yes                yes
  dev-team-2            2           yes                 yes                yes
  qa1                   2           yes                 yes                yes
  pipeman              15           yes                 yes                yes
  liveqa               14           yes                 yes                yes

Instruction block 537-749 chars ahead of a ~1,200-char task. It reaches the role through the launch, never through an agent file — the named risk, avoided.

The wording is right too, and that is not a small thing here: it says matching "has not been demonstrated to tolerate" an absolute-path variant, rather than asserting it doesn't. After sprint 26 that distinction is the house style, and you kept it.

REQ 3 — instructedCommandForms is parsed from the record's own allowedTools value, present as an empty array rather than omitted when there is no grant. An operator holding only stderr can read the grant and the forms side by side.

One honest limit on that field, worth stating for LiveQA: it reports what the grant parses to, not a readback of the prompt. If the prepending ever broke, the record would still list forms and would be confidently wrong about what the role was told. That is not a live defect — your Req 4 subprocess test asserts the real prompt contains each form, and it caught my no-prepend mutation — but "instructed" claims slightly more than the field measures, and the protection lives in a test rather than in the record.

REQ 5 — confirmed properly, not by eye. Serialized HEADLESS_PERMISSION_PROFILES from each commit's own module: 170e7258f788763a… at 82cb7fe and at 17461bb. Byte-identical. No pattern widened, no grant added. Also checked every Bash entry across all six profiles ends with a space-wildcard, so extractGrantedCommandForms' regex covers all of them — a non-wildcard entry would be silently omitted from the instruction, but none exists today.

TESTS — falsified, three ways, against a full repo copy with a green baseline first:
  instruction not prepended        -> 7 tests FAIL, including the Req 4 subprocess test
  instructedCommandForms hardcoded -> 2 tests FAIL
  parser returns only the first form -> 2 tests FAIL
And the recomputation worry about expectedPromptFor is answered by that first result: the five pre-existing tests it feeds did fail when the instruction stopped being prepended, so the helper is not a tautology, it just computes the expectation by a different route than the code under test.

SUITE: ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED. ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED. TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED, "Installed 0.2.4".

================================================================
YOUR SCOPE FLAG — RIGHT AGAIN, PREMISE CHECKED
================================================================

npm view: 0.2.3 is published and `latest` points at it. Versions are immutable, so package.json at 0.2.3 would fail Pipeman's publish, and Reqs 1 and 3 both have LiveQA criteria that require a real published install. Necessary for the sprint's own acceptance criteria. Flagging rather than deciding silently is right; this is the second sprint running where the Requirements list omitted a bump every comparable prior sprint carried, so the thing to fix is the template, not your judgment.

CARRIED, INFORMATIONAL
- `root` is half-threaded in headlessLaunchArgs (see above). Pre-existing since sprint 12, harmless in production, and directly in the way of Req 4's fix.
- Long-carried: every allowlist entry other than git and npm remains inferred; the empty-string ownedRepository declaration still falls through silently; who commits a QA1 verdict is still Master Controller's open question from sprint 27.

RECOMMENDATION

Back to dev_build for Req 4 only. Thread `root`, add the divergence test, re-run /sprint-qa1 31. Reqs 1, 2, 3 and 5 are done and I don't need to see them again — hand me back the one thing.
